title: Identity and birthplace; parents' origins
description: Betty Virginia Smith identifies herself as Betty Virginia Tease, born February 25, 1938, in Spokane, Washington, raised on a farm near Worley, Idaho. She discusses her parents' English and German heritage, her mother's work as a hired girl before marriage, and her father's birth in Fairfield, Washington, in 1905.

title: Father's wheat farm; family size
description: She describes her father John Henry Teese's 160-acre wheat farm, noting it was one of the smallest in the area, and his later carpentry work. She names her sister Arlene and begins discussing her immediate family.

title: Hunter outfitting; sons in logging
description: Betty explains that her husband Robert Smith is a logger and hunting outfitter who traps bobcats and coyotes in winter. She names her five children, noting that sons Terry and Teddy work in logging, and describes Terry's work as an extra in the film Breakheart Pass with Charles Bronson and Ben Johnson.

title: Traditional skills; rural vs urban life
description: She lists skills learned on the farm and in marriage: driving tractor, milking cows, carpentry, electrical wiring, canning, and sewing. She contrasts rural life favorably against city life, citing safety, freedom for children, and low-cost recreation like swimming and picnicking by the river.

title: Childhood poverty; homemade clothing
description: Betty contrasts her isolated farm childhood with her current social family life, recalling that company was a rare event. She describes the poverty of her early years, wearing dresses and coats made by her mother, and receiving only two pairs of shoes annually.

title: Childhood games; limited schooling
description: She recalls playing dolls with her sister Arlene, creating imaginary teenage personas named Peggy and others, and inventing boyfriends. She describes her two years of high school in a small school of thirty-five students before quitting to marry at age 16.

title: Meeting Bob; courtship
description: Betty recounts meeting Robert Smith through her sister's correspondence with his brother, involving a mix-up with both brothers before she and Bob became serious. She describes their long-distance courtship, his 180-mile drives to visit, and a trip where they got stuck in the mud overnight in his pickup.

title: Marriage expectations; radio communication
description: She states her marital expectations of making a good home and being happy, noting they have succeeded despite rough times. The conversation shifts to the two-way radio her husband and sons use while bear hunting, with the noise of the radio audible in the background.

title: Childbirth choices; family planning
description: Betty discusses having her first children in a hospital and the last one at home, attended by an elderly doctor she persuaded to assist. She explains her decisions about spacing and number of children, wanting to avoid the loneliness she experienced, and her disappointment at having three boys before finally getting a girl.

title: Children's futures; economic contributions
description: She expects her sons to follow their father into logging and guiding. She describes her economic contributions through canning, baking, sewing for pay, selling animal hides, and saving to buy a dishwasher.

title: Modern conveniences; career alternatives
description: Betty discusses acquiring a dishwasher and other modern appliances, noting that without them she would have to chop wood herself. She considers what she would do if her husband died, mentioning she would like to be a beautician but doubts she could support the family alone.

title: Housewifery advice; workload
description: She has never displayed work at a county fair. She advises young women to learn cooking, sewing, and money management, putting family first, and criticizes some modern young women as spoiled. She admits to sometimes feeling overworked when hunters are present, but views it as part of supporting her husband's business.

title: Farm kitchen cooperation; childhood chores
description: Betty recalls cooking for uncles and cousins during haying season back on the farm, with big roasts and pies. She lists her childhood chores: feeding chickens, gathering eggs, carrying wood, milking cows, separating cream, and washing the separator.

title: Family home; church membership
description: She describes her father moving and remodeling an old schoolhouse into their warm family home. She identifies herself as a Jehovah's Witness but explains she does not join community clubs because she is busy at home.

title: Close family; childrearing principles
description: Betty describes her family as close-knit, with her husband preferring drive-ins to theaters. She discusses raising her boys without drugs or alcohol through Biblical principles and example-setting, noting they have never been in trouble.

title: Reading materials; rebuilding house
description: She lists magazines the family receives: hunting and fishing magazines for Bob, Redbook and McCall's for herself, and Bible study aids. She recounts their house burning down after five years of marriage without insurance and rebuilding it themselves.

title: Social security; medical costs
description: Bob pays into social security and draws unemployment in winter, but they lack medical insurance and face difficult medical bills. They are considering hospital insurance due to high hospital costs.

title: Television preferences; nature programs
description: She prefers crocheting to watching TV but enjoys Animal World, music shows like Mac Davis and the Irish Rovers, and the truck-driving series Moving On. She avoids watching the news because she finds it depressing.

title: Daily greetings; outdoor education
description: Bob greets her by asking how her day went when he returns from the woods. He takes the children steelhead fishing, teaches them gun safety with real guns rather than BB guns, and involves them in hunting, trapping, and identifying animal tracks.

title: Gender roles; outdoor skills
description: She affirms that daughter Becky is included in outdoor activities like fishing and wildlife viewing when possible, though she cannot keep up with walking. The family picks berries and mushrooms together, and all children have learned to fish.

title: Managing the hunting business; travel limitations
description: Betty Virginia Smith explains how she manages the business operations of Bob's hunting trade while he distrusts stores and shopping. She notes they rarely travel together, with Bob's trips centered on hunting and her staying home with the children.

title: Elk hunting memories; wild game diet
description: She recalls her past elk hunting experiences, including shooting one herself and receiving help dressing it. She describes their reliance on deer and elk for meat, trading bear hunts for beef, and trying cougar meat despite Bob's aversion to bear.

title: Butchering and processing game meat
description: Betty Virginia Smith details her self-taught methods for cutting elk meat into steaks, roasts, and hamburger, having the market grind the meat, and managing the use of hides and organs. She explains the twelve-hour process of breaking down a large elk and the network of hunting dogs they feed.

title: Kitchen routines; reasons for settling in Kuski
description: She describes sharpening knives, cooking from scratch without restaurants nearby, and preparing meals even after long butchering sessions. She explains she moved to Kuski because it was Bob's home and grew to love the mountain country.

title: Nez Perce neighbor; local race relations
description: She describes their friendship with Charlie, their Nez Perce neighbor who shares gardening knowledge, and how his grandchildren play with her daughters. She discusses the community's racial tensions regarding alcohol and stereotypes about Native Americans.

title: Charlie's Indian regalia; cultural artifacts
description: Betty Virginia Smith describes examining Charlie's collection of valuable Nez Perce clothing, including a dress weighted with beads made from steelhead vertebrae and a chief's bonnet inherited from his grandfather. She discusses the significance of eagle feather imagery and handcrafted silverwork.

title: Hazards of professional hunting; lifestyle acceptance
description: She reflects on the dangers of Bob's work with wounded bears and aggressive cougars, the injuries their dogs have sustained, and her gradual acceptance of the risks inherent in his profession. She concludes by noting how she changed her social expectations upon marrying him.
